toc.title: Undo changes you have not committed
Undo local commits: amend and reset
Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick

html:
1Undo changes you have not committed

Every undo starts with one question: where is the change right now? Git keeps it in the working tree, in the staging area, in a local commit, or on the remote. Each place has its own undo command, as the figure shows.

Command What it does
git restore <file> Discards the edit in the working tree. Git never saved it, so there is no undo
git restore --staged <file> Unstages the file; the edit stays in the working tree
git restore --source=HEAD~1 <file> Brings back the file as it was in an older commit, as an unstaged change
git clean -n, then git clean -f Previews, then deletes untracked files

git restore does not know untracked files, so git restore scratch.txt fails. Older guides use git checkout -- <file>, which still works. git clean refuses to run without -f. By default it keeps untracked directories (-d includes them) and ignored files (-x includes them).

Try it. cart.txt is staged and scratch.txt is a new file. Unstage, discard, then clean. The restore commands print nothing.

git status -s
git restore --staged cart.txt
git restore cart.txt
git clean -n
git clean -f

M  cart.txt
?? scratch.txt
Would remove scratch.txt
Removing scratch.txt
Tip

. Always run git clean -n before git clean -f. Deleted untracked files are gone for good, and the dry run shows exactly which ones.

2Undo local commits: amend and reset

If the commit is not pushed, you may rewrite it. git commit --amend replaces the last commit: stage a forgotten file, then amend. git reset <mode> <commit> moves the branch back, and the mode decides what happens to the changes.

Mode Branch Staging area Working tree
--soft Moved back Keeps the undone changes staged Unchanged
--mixed (default) Moved back Reset: changes unstaged Unchanged
--hard Moved back Reset Reset: changes gone

Try it. The same commit, undone three ways. Each git reset --hard returns to the commit d8a95e7, and your hash will differ.

git reset -q --soft HEAD~1 && git status -s
git reset -q --hard d8a95e7
git reset -q --mixed HEAD~1 && git status -s
git reset -q --hard d8a95e7
git reset -q --hard HEAD~1 && git status -s

M  cart.txt
 M cart.txt

The soft reset shows the file staged, the mixed reset shows it modified but unstaged, and the hard reset prints nothing because the tree is clean again. A hard reset also throws away uncommitted edits to tracked files, and it leaves untracked files alone.

Tip

. Use --soft or --mixed to keep your work, and --hard only when you mean to throw it away. Uncommitted changes are in no commit, so even the reflog cannot return them.

3Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick

Once a commit is pushed, do not rewrite it. In the lab, Ada reset her branch and committed again: her push was rejected as a non-fast-forward. git revert <hash> instead adds a new commit that undoes the old one. History stays intact, so the push is normal and teammates pull it as a fast-forward.

Try it. Revert the last commit.

git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log --oneline

[main 1a81873] Revert "Change cart"
1a81873 Revert "Change cart"
d8a95e7 Change cart
d06c1e8 Add cart
c95e906 Add README

The message says "This reverts commit" and the hash. The original commit stays in the log.

Reverting a merge. A merge commit has two parents, so Git cannot guess which side to keep. It stops with "is a merge but no -m option was given". Add -m 1: parent 1 is the branch you merged into, so the work that the merged branch brought is removed and the rest stays. The old history stays, too. Merging the same branch again now says "Already up to date" and brings nothing. To get the feature back, revert the revert.

Cherry-pick. git cherry-pick <hash> copies one commit from another branch onto the current one, with the same message and a new hash. -x adds "(cherry picked from commit ...)" to the message. If both sides changed the same lines, it conflicts like a merge, and git cherry-pick --abort puts everything back.

Tip

. Pushed means revert, not rewrite. A revert is a normal new commit that everyone can pull.

4Stash: park work without committing

Stash saves your uncommitted changes on a shelf and gives you a clean working tree. Use it when you must switch branches in the middle of something.

Command What it does
git stash push -m "text" Saves tracked changes with a label
git stash push -u Also saves untracked files, which stay behind by default
git stash list Lists entries, newest first: stash@{0}
git stash pop Re-applies the newest entry and removes it
git stash apply Re-applies it and keeps the entry
git stash drop Deletes the entry
git stash branch <name> New branch from the commit the stash was made on, applies it, drops it

Try it. Park an edit, then bring it back.

git stash push -m "wip cart"
git stash list
git stash pop

Saved working directory and index state On main: wip cart
stash@{0}: On main: wip cart
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (96c7347c1baac60a61979a64217d923969776f79)

If the file changed on the branch in the meantime, pop stops with a conflict and keeps the entry, so nothing is lost. stash branch is the clean way out: the new branch starts where the stash began, so the changes apply without a conflict.

Tip

. Give every stash a label with -m, and prefer pop over leaving a long list. Entries called "WIP on main" are impossible to tell apart a week later.

5The safety net: the reflog

The reflog is a local diary of every place HEAD and each branch pointed. A commit that no branch reaches is not deleted yet, and the reflog still names it. It exists only in your clone and is cleaned up after a while.

Try it. Throw two commits away, then take them back.

git reset --hard HEAD~2
git reflog
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}

HEAD is now at 4b90fda Add README
4b90fda HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
1388219 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add checkout
075853f HEAD@{2}: commit: Add cart
HEAD is now at 1388219 Add checkout

HEAD@{1} means "where HEAD was one move ago". If you did other things in between, read the list and use the hash.

A deleted branch. git branch -d refuses a branch with unmerged commits. git branch -D deletes it and prints Deleted branch feature/wishlist (was c139300). That hash is your way back: git branch feature/wishlist c139300.

What do I want to undo Use
An edit, not staged git restore <file>
A staged file git restore --staged <file>
Last commit, wrong message or file, not pushed git commit --amend
Commits not pushed, keep the work git reset --soft or --mixed
Commits not pushed, throw them away git reset --hard HEAD~N
A commit already pushed git revert <hash>
A lost commit or branch git reflog, then git branch or git reset --hard
Tip

. When something vanishes, stop and run git reflog before anything else. The commit is almost always still there.

6Practice Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1git status -s shows M cart.txt and ?? scratch.txt. You want to unstage cart.txt and keep your edit. Which command does that?

  • Agit restore cart.txt, which discards the edit
  • Bgit restore --staged cart.txt, which unstages it
  • Cgit clean -f, which deletes untracked files
  • Dgit reset --hard, which resets index and files
Show the answer

Answer: B. --staged removes the file from the staging area and leaves the edit in the working tree.

S2You committed to main by mistake and have not pushed. You want the commit undone and its changes left staged. Which command fits?

  • Agit reset --hard HEAD~1, which deletes the changes
  • Bgit reset --mixed HEAD~1, which leaves them unstaged
  • Cgit reset --soft HEAD~1, which leaves them staged
  • Dgit revert HEAD, which adds a new undoing commit
Show the answer

Answer: C. --soft moves the branch back and keeps the changes in the staging area.

S3A bad commit is on main, and teammates have already pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?

  • Agit reset --hard HEAD~1, then git push --force
  • Bgit commit --amend, then a normal git push
  • Cgit stash, then git stash drop on main
  • Dgit revert <hash>, then a normal git push
Show the answer

Answer: D. A revert is a new commit on top, so nobody's history is rewritten and the push is accepted.

S4git revert HEAD on a merge commit prints "is a merge but no -m option was given". What do you run next?

  • Agit revert -m 1 HEAD, which keeps the first parent's side
  • Bgit revert --no-edit HEAD, which retries without an editor
  • Cgit cherry-pick -m 1 HEAD, which copies the merge again
  • Dgit merge --abort, which stops the failed revert
Show the answer

Answer: A. Parent 1 is the branch that was merged into, so -m 1 removes only what the merged branch brought.

S5git branch -D feature/wishlist printed Deleted branch feature/wishlist (was c139300). You need the branch back. What do you run?

  • ARestore the branch with git restore feature/wishlist
  • BRecreate it with git branch feature/wishlist c139300
  • CBring it back with git stash branch feature/wishlist
  • DUndo the deletion with git revert feature/wishlist
Show the answer

Answer: B. The printed hash is the old tip, and git branch <name> <hash> creates a branch there again.

S6You edited cart.txt and created a new untracked file notes.txt. You run git stash push -m wip. What does git status show?

  • ABoth files are stashed, and the tree is clean
  • BOnly notes.txt is stashed, and the edit stays
  • CNothing is stashed because notes.txt is untracked
  • Dcart.txt is stashed, and notes.txt is untracked
Show the answer

Answer: D. A stash takes tracked changes only, unless you add -u.

6.2 Recall questions

R1Which command unstages a file but keeps the edit?

Show the answer

git restore --staged <file>.

R2Which option of git clean previews what would be removed?

Show the answer

-n, the dry run.

R3Which command replaces the last unpushed commit with a corrected one?

Show the answer

git commit --amend.

R4What does git revert do to history?

Show the answer

It adds a new commit that undoes an older one and rewrites nothing.

R5Which command copies one commit onto your current branch?

Show the answer

git cherry-pick <hash>.

R6Which command lists where HEAD has been, so you can find a lost commit?

Show the answer

git reflog.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Discard and unstage git restore <file> discards; git restore --staged <file> unstages
Clean git clean -n previews; -f deletes untracked files; -d directories; -x ignored files
Amend replaces the last commit; only before you push
Reset --soft keeps changes staged; --mixed keeps them unstaged; --hard throws them away
Revert new commit that undoes an old one; for pushed work; a merge needs -m 1
Cherry-pick copies one commit with a new hash; -x notes the source; --abort on conflict
Stash push -m, -u, list, pop, apply, drop, branch
Reflog local history of HEAD; recover with reset --hard HEAD@{N} or git branch name hash
